newsitem.title: USA: Columbia Gas sets market test participation.
newsitem.headline: Columbia Gas sets market test participation.

text.p: Columbia Gas System Inc said its pipeline units Friday petitioned the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to allow them to participate in a pilot program that will permit market forces, instead of regulation, to set the prices for certain natural gas transportation services.

The pilot program, which was proposed by FERC on July 31, will allow the use of market pricing rather than regulated rates to set fees that natural gas shippers can charge when they rent to other shippers the capacity, or space, they hold on interstate pipelines.
The program is expected to run through the 1996-97 winter, Columbia Gas noted.

Catherine Good Abbott, chief executive of Columbia's Columbia Transmission and Columbia Gulf subsidiaries, said FERC's experimental program "creates a forum to show that there is competition for pipeline capacity in what is known as the secondary market.
"By introducing this program, the commission is showing that it is prepared to test new approaches for pricing pipeline capacity in light of today's competitive marketplace.
"Columbia is delighted to be among the first to volunteer to participate," Abbott said.
The secondary market deals with transportation services such as capacity release, interruptible and short-term firm transportation, the company explained.

Capacity release allows local distribution companies and other shippers who hold capacity on pipelines under firm contracts to release, or loan, that capacity to other shippers. Currently, FERC rules cap the price that capacity holders can charge for the released capacity.
The pilot program will remove the price cap for deliveries to qualifying-LDC markets, allowing market-based pricing for transactions into those markets, Columbia Gas said.
In a joint filing, Columbia Gas Transmission Corp and Columbia Gulf Transmission Co said several of their local distribution company customers asked them to participate.
Those companies will make separate filings with FERC to show that they conform to the requirements of the pilot program, Columbia noted.
